subsystems.name: Integrated circuit
subsystems.role: stores the identity credential and runs cryptographic authentication.

subsystems.name: Antenna
subsystems.role: harvests power from the reader's radio field and sends data back.

subsystems.name: Encapsulation
subsystems.role: protects the electronics from body fluids and prevents tissue rejection.

subsystems.name: Reader infrastructure
subsystems.role: powers the implant and verifies its identity.

buildSteps.title: Design the chip
buildSteps.detail: Engineers lay out a CMOS integrated circuit with a secure element that can perform cryptographic challenges within the tiny power budget of a passive tag.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the silicon
buildSteps.detail: The chip is made in a semiconductor foundry using standard CMOS processes, then diced and tested.

buildSteps.title: Wind the antenna
buildSteps.detail: A fine copper coil is wound around a ferrite core and soldered to the chip to form a resonant circuit tuned to 13.56 MHz.

buildSteps.title: Encapsulate
buildSteps.detail: The assembly is placed inside a biocompatible glass capsule, which is filled with medical-grade epoxy and sealed under vacuum or inert gas.

buildSteps.title: Sterilize and test
buildSteps.detail: Capsules are sterilized (e.g., by gamma radiation or ethylene oxide) and tested for read range, data integrity, and hermeticity.

buildSteps.title: Implant
buildSteps.detail: A medical professional injects the capsule under the skin, typically in the web between thumb and forefinger, using a sterile applicator.

buildSteps.title: Provision and enroll
buildSteps.detail: The implant is scanned, a unique cryptographic key is written, and its identifier is registered in the access control or medical record system.

prerequisites.why: defines the radio protocol and security features for contactless authentication.
long-term implants like pacemakers use similar glass and coatings to avoid rejection.
smart cards and phones already perform the same cryptographic authentication.
medical implants are routinely placed under the skin, though voluntary identity chips are not yet standard care.

pathway.milestone: hobbyist and small-office access control using off-the-shelf implants
pathway.unlocks: proof that passive implants can replace cards and fobs for some users.

pathway.milestone: regulated use in high-security facilities with multi-factor authentication
pathway.unlocks: stronger identity assurance than a card alone.

pathway.milestone: integration with electronic health records for emergency access
pathway.unlocks: instant medical history for unconscious patients, if privacy rules allow.

pathway.milestone: combining implants with biometric sensors and advanced cryptography
pathway.unlocks: continuous authentication without any external token.
